Chapter Two: When and How to Begin the Process
So, when should you actually start the journey of death cleaning? Well, there’s no magic age or single life event that says, “now’s the time.” Even though the term might sound like something you’d only consider much later in life, it’s really useful at any stage of adulthood. Sometimes, the idea pops into your mind after a move, when you’re downsizing, or maybe after seeing what happens when a loved one passes away. The best moment to begin? It’s when you feel that nudge—when the thought first appears. And it’s so much easier if you approach it calmly, with a sense of readiness, instead of waiting for a crisis or feeling rushed.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the emotional world tied up in our belongings. Every object might carry a memory, a dream, or a reminder of someone important. Acknowledging those feelings is the first real step. It helps you be kind to yourself and realistic about what you’re ready to let go of. Think of it not as erasing your past, but as honoring it—while making space for what matters now, and what’s ahead.
If you’re wondering where to start, here’s a tip: pick a category or area that feels easy. Don’t dive straight into the things that tug hardest at your heartstrings. Instead, try beginning with something practical—maybe your clothes, kitchenware, or a stack of old books. These less sentimental items help you practice, build confidence, and get some momentum going. That way, when you’re ready, the more meaningful objects won’t feel quite so daunting.
You might picture the process as a set of concentric circles. The outermost ring holds the items you hardly ever think about—things with little emotional pull. The closer you get to the center, the more personal and treasured the items become. By working from the outside in, you’re gently training yourself to make thoughtful, loving decisions about what to keep and what to let go.
And remember, it doesn’t have to be all serious. Keeping a sense of humor and openness makes the whole experience lighter. Death cleaning isn’t a punishment or some heavy chore—it’s a chance to reflect, to share stories, and even to laugh at all the little quirks and memories your things hold. Inviting a trusted friend or family member to join you can turn the process into a team effort, making it supportive and even fun, instead of a lonely task.
So, what are some practical ways to get started? Here are a few guidelines:
- Begin with items that are easy to say goodbye to, like duplicates or things you haven’t used in years.
- Set aside regular, manageable chunks of time, instead of trying to tackle everything at once.
- Use the opportunity to reconnect with memories, and share stories with others as you sort through your things.
- And most importantly, be patient with yourself. Some choices will take time, and that’s perfectly okay.
By embracing death cleaning as a gentle, ongoing journey, you can avoid feeling overwhelmed and make decisions that truly reflect your values and relationships. And honestly, just taking that first small step—no matter how tiny it seems—sets you up for a more intentional, peaceful way of living.
